title: Rebuilding match physical insight after relegation
text: Relegation removed the league data feed that match physical insight depended on, and the club’s legacy data ecosystem went with it. Practitioners and stakeholders still expected the same insight the morning after a match. How do you keep delivering match physical insight, with context, when the data it was built on has gone?

title: Rebuilding match physical insight after relegation
text:
The approach
Two sources were left, and neither was a like-for-like replacement. GPS was collected at every match but had mainly been used in training. League-wide broadcast tracking covered every team, but with different speed zones. Rather than force one source to do everything, I designed a report around what each could honestly support:

A contextualised GPS report for player decisions. This became the core product, ready within 2 hours of the final whistle.
A broadcast tracking trend report for team-level context. It sets our physical output against the opposition and the league. Because its speed zones aren’t directly comparable with GPS, it informs the picture rather than driving decisions.

title: Rebuilding match physical insight after relegation
text:
What I built
The GPS report started as match summaries and grew into a full contextual breakdown:

A possession state model, built from the event data provider’s match events, that splits every player’s output into in possession, out of possession and ball out of play.
15-minute blocks, showing how each player’s output changed across the match.
Time alignment of the GPS and event data feeds by their Unix timestamps, so every metre of running is tied to what was happening in the game at that moment.
Validation of the possession tagging against match video, across a sample of five matches, before anyone relied on it.
An automated pipeline, from raw files to a finished report on the practitioner’s computer, leaving room for them to add their own context.

I released it in three layers and only launched each one once staff trusted the one before. That kept adoption high: nobody was asked to change how they worked on the strength of numbers they hadn’t yet learned to read.

title: Rebuilding match physical insight after relegation
text:
The outcome
The GPS report now lands within 2 hours of the final whistle instead of after a 10–12 hour wait, and with more context than the league feed ever gave.
That speed changes decisions. When a substitute who played 30 minutes shows a sprint load closer to a full 90, staff see it before MD+1 is planned and can adjust the session the same evening, rather than finding out after it.

title: Slate and Signal: one visual language for every chart, app and deck
text:
All my career I’ve had a club theme or university colours to base my visuals and decks on. When I decided to build a portfolio, I was a bit flummoxed. This work needed to look distinct to me, and there was nothing to borrow.
A consistent theme matters a lot when delivering insight, because charts made in different tools drift apart. A ggplot in a report, a Shiny app and a slide deck each end up with their own colours and fonts, and colour starts to mean nothing in particular. The reader has to work out what to look at every time.
I wanted one set of rules that every output inherits automatically, so the design decisions are made once and the reader’s attention goes straight to the point.

title: Slate and Signal: one visual language for every chart, app and deck
text:
The approach
Having been through Andy Kirk’s data visualisation training, I care as much about every chart telling a story as about charts looking consistent. Slate and Signal is built on that. The design decisions are made once, and each one exists to point the reader at what matters.

One accent, everything else grey. The eye picks out whatever is different before the reader has consciously started looking. So signal teal (#009999) is kept for the one point of the chart, and everything that supports it sits in context grey (#B8C0C9).
Titles state the takeaway. “High-speed running by player” names the topic. “Player 3 is back above their normal range” tells you what to think, and the chart then backs it up.
Defined once, used everywhere. Every colour, font and size lives in a single tokens file. That one file generates the R theme, the Quarto styles, the Python helpers and the Streamlit configuration, so a report, an app and a deck can’t drift apart.
Colours keep their meaning. Categorical colours follow a fixed order, so the same series is the same colour in every chart. Status colours are only ever used for status.
Readable by everyone. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) set a minimum contrast between text and its background so people with low vision can still read it. Level AA, the standard most organisations work to, asks for a ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text. Every text colour here meets it, which is why links use a darker teal (#007A7A) than the chart accent.
Safe for colour blindness. Around 1 in 12 men has some form of colour vision deficiency, most often difficulty telling red from green. In a coaching staff, that’s likely to be someone in the room. Every categorical colour was checked under simulations of the three main types (deutan, protan and tritan) so no two series look the same. Status colours never rely on colour alone either: in range, monitor and out of range always come with an icon and a word.

Inter carries the text and JetBrains Mono the code. Every rule has a light and a dark version, so the system holds in either theme.

title: Slate and Signal: one visual language for every chart, app and deck
text:
The palette









Slate gives structure, signal teal is the single accent, and a cool grey called context is used for everything that supports the message rather than being the message. Status colours are reserved for state (in range, monitor, out of range) and always appear with an icon or a word, never colour alone.

title: Slate and Signal: one visual language for every chart, app and deck
section: The core rule: grey for context, signal for the point
text:
The core rule: grey for context, signal for the point
The same data, drawn with default settings and then with the system. The default gives every player a different colour, so nothing stands out. With the system, the one player the chart is about is the only thing in colour, and the title says what the reader should take away.

BeforeAfter

title: Slate and Signal: one visual language for every chart, app and deck
text:
Style as code
The rules live in one tokens file and are packaged for each tool I use, so a chart picks up the system with a line or two:
source("R/theme_md.R")

ggplot(df, aes(session, hsr, colour = player)) +
  geom_line() +
  md_highlight("Player 3") +   # grey for everyone except the focus
  theme_md()                   # type, gridlines, titles and captions
The same values drive a matplotlib and Plotly theme for Python, a Streamlit configuration, a Quarto slide theme, a PowerPoint template and this website.

title: Slate and Signal: one visual language for every chart, app and deck
text:
What I’d do next
Package the R theme as a small installable package with its own tests, so colleagues could adopt it with library(mdtheme) and get updates automatically.

title: Building a player load monitoring tool
text:
Context

The Vizathon
In March 2025, Chelsea FC’s Performance Insights team ran an open vizathon with one brief: create the most compelling physical performance interface for elite football players and their coaches. Entrants worked from a mock dataset covering load, physical development, recovery and individual priorities, and the competition drew 124 entries from 27 countries.


The data
Four files describe a single player. The values are simulated, but the structure mirrors what a club’s performance department collects. This tool uses the GPS file; the recovery file feeds a companion research question on how recovery responds to load.








File
What it holds
Coverage




GPS
Daily training and match load: distance, high-speed running, accelerations, heart rate, with each day labelled by its position in the match week
August 2022 to April 2025


Physical capability
Benchmark scores for 20 combinations of movement, quality and force expression
July 2023 to March 2025


Recovery status
Daily scores across six categories, from sleep and soreness to blood markers
July 2023 to March 2025


Individual priority areas
Three development targets agreed by the player and staff
March to May 2025





The club around the data
The physical values are simulated, but the fixtures follow Chelsea’s real calendar, and that calendar was unusually turbulent.

For load monitoring, the calendar matters as much as the numbers. A season with European football means more two-match weeks and shorter gaps to recover and build load between games; a season without it gives longer, more structured training weeks. Three coaching changes in one season would also mean three different training philosophies. Because this data is simulated I won’t read coaching effects into it, but the tool is designed so that a real dataset could be split by these periods.

title: Building a player load monitoring tool
section: What the tool needs to answer
text:
What the tool needs to answer
Staff don’t need every GPS metric every day. They need a few questions answered quickly:

Is today’s load normal for this day of the match week? Each session is compared with the player’s own norm for that match-week day, so an MD-1 is judged against other MD-1s rather than against a match.
How is the week building? Rolling load over the last 7 and 28 days shows whether the player is building, holding or dropping relative to their recent history.
What did the match ask of them? Match load set against the player’s typical full-match output, so a short appearance with a high sprint load stands out.

High-speed running above 21 km/h is the lead measure, with total distance, accelerations and decelerations, and session duration alongside.

title: Building a player load monitoring tool
text:
What’s in the app







Page
What it answers




Overview
Where the player is today: how many metrics are outside their normal range, the latest session, and the last 28 days of load


Profile
Who the player is, the current status of every metric, and what each type of day typically looks like


Longitudinal
How load has built over any period: daily, against the adaptive range, or as rolling 7- and 28-day load, with sessions outside their range marked


Session check
One session against its normal ranges, against the last 10 sessions of the same type, and the recovery scores that followed

What every metric means and how the app uses it

title: About
text:
The best analysis is the one people use, and keep using. In elite sport, the success of an insight comes down to two things. The first is staying close to the people asking the question, so the work answers what they need now and anticipates what comes next. The second is keeping it simple and clear, because decisions are made fast. That’s why my work starts with a performance question, not a dataset.
I’ve spent six years in elite football data, working my way up from an MSc studentship in 2019 to leading data insight for the Sport Science and Medical departments at Leicester City. I taught myself to code early, driven by an instinct that the processes around me could be automated or done better. That instinct shaped the pipelines and processes I’ve built since, so practitioners get what they need, when they need it.
I take pride in how results are communicated. Every visualisation and report is built to turn analysis into a clear message stakeholders can act on. When relegation cost us the league’s data feed, I rebuilt match reporting from our own GPS data, and staff had it within two hours of the final whistle instead of the next day.
My PhD, completed this year, rests on one idea: in physical performance, context is everything. A number means little in isolation, because so much of it is shaped by the game around it. I set the research up to feed straight into my day-to-day work, and it taught me how to frame a performance question: what needs to be measured, which factors contribute, and how to back the answer with mathematical rigour.
I’ve line managed data analysts, developing both their technical skills and how they communicate. Analysts I’ve managed have gone on to roles in sport science departments at other clubs, and that’s what I’m proudest of.
I’m still developing my skill set. Right now I’m most interested in fully automated pipelines, the kind our data engineer builds, and in how containerised projects with automated reporting can give data staff their time back. I’m also exploring how AI tools can shape my work. They clearly speed up the build and delivery of insight, so more of my time goes on the question and less on the plumbing, while the judgement stays with me. I’m also continuing to work on how I communicate with stakeholders, because even the best insight has to land to be used.

Away from work
I grew up in the Peak District, which gave me a love of nature and the hills. It’s probably why Eryri and the Lake District make my list of places to visit every year. Cycling is my main passion, with the odd parkrun thrown in, and data follows me here as well: I use power, pace and heart rate response to govern my training. Football and rugby are different. I watch as much as I can, but as a fan rather than an analyst, and I might be the only data person in football who doesn’t play Fantasy Premier League.
